analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for companies' offshoring costs and expands aid for laid-off service workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: referred to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2004 with zero cosponsors, it sat there until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped companies from deducting the expenses of moving American jobs overseas — training foreign replacement workers, shipping equipment abroad, and closing domestic facilities. It would have extended trade adjustment assistance (federal retraining and income support for workers hurt by trade) to service and IT workers, not just factory workers, created a wage insurance program paying half the gap between a laid-off worker's old and new wages for up to two years, and made the health insurance tax credit for trade-displaced workers more generous and easier to use. It also gave a legal shield to corporate officers who decide to keep jobs in the United States.
analysis.who_benefits: Displaced service-sector, IT, and public-agency workers who are currently shut out of trade adjustment assistance would gain retraining, income support, and health coverage. Workers who find new jobs at lower pay could get up to $10,000 over two years in wage insurance. Workers in the trade-adjustment health credit program would get faster reimbursement, a bigger subsidy (75% of premiums instead of 65%), and no coverage gap while waiting for certification.

how_it_helps.text: Companies could no longer deduct any expense connected with moving production or services from the US to other countries, including costs of training the foreign replacement workers, transporting property abroad, and closing domestic facilities.
Trade adjustment assistance would cover service-sector firms and public agencies for the first time, and retraining funding would double from $220 million to $440 million.

A wage insurance program would pay 50% of the difference between a displaced worker's old and new wages for up to two years, capped at $10,000, for workers rehired within 26 weeks at $50,000 a year or less.

The health insurance tax credit for trade-displaced workers would rise from 65% to 75% of premiums, be paid in advance for months before certification, cover spouses of Medicare-eligible workers, and be aligned with COBRA so coverage would not lapse.
Corporate officers and directors who decide to keep jobs in the United States would get a 'business judgment' safe harbor so they could not be sued by shareholders for that decision.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that move US jobs overseas would lose their federal tax deductions for doing so, and the Treasury would bear the cost of expanded retraining ($440 million), wage insurance payments, and the larger health credit. Shareholder plaintiffs would lose some ability to sue directors who decline to offshore.

drawbacks.text: Wage insurance pays companies' new lower wages a subsidy in effect: it can encourage displaced workers to accept reduced pay faster, with taxpayers covering half the gap up to $10,000 per worker.

The business judgment safe harbor protects directors from shareholder lawsuits whenever they invoke keeping jobs at home, even if that rationale masks other reasons — it trades shareholder accountability for an incentive the tax code was already designed to supply.

Denying deductions for offshoring expenses raises the after-tax cost of relocating without prohibiting it, and critics of such measures argue it puts US multinationals at a competitive disadvantage and adds compliance complexity to the tax code.
The bill has no stated funding source for its new spending, so expanded retraining, wage insurance, and the richer health credit would add to the deficit or require offsetting cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers displaced by offshoring — a group explicitly shut out of the existing trade-adjustment system, which covers only manufacturing — the bill offered substantial, concrete help: a doubled retraining budget, wage insurance, and a health credit that actually covers enough of the premium to be usable. The costs are real but modest by tax-bill standards: some lost deductions for firms that offshore, several hundred million dollars in new assistance spending, and a somewhat loosened standard for shareholder suits against directors. The wage insurance design is the weakest piece, since it can subsidize lower wages rather than restore them.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced it in June 2004 and the Senate Finance Committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Wyden introduced the Keeping American Jobs at Home Act on June 16, 2004, with introductory remarks in the Congressional Record.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, where it remained; no markup, hearing, or floor vote is recorded in its action history.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill received no further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that move US jobs overseas kept the ability to deduct the costs of doing so, since the deduction ban never became law. Service-sector and IT workers displaced by offshoring remained outside the trade-adjustment system. The Finance Committee's do-nothing outcome preserved the existing tax and trade-adjustment status quo.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor; no other senator joined him.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 16, 2004 and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill, no senator of either party cosponsored it, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Companies that offshore US jobs (business services, IT, and manufacturing offshorers)
industries.note: The bill would have ended federal tax deductions for expenses tied to moving American jobs abroad, including training foreign replacement workers. Its defeat left those subsidies in place.

industries.industry: Health insurers selling coverage to trade-displaced workers
industries.note: The bill increases the tax credit that pays insurers' premiums for trade-displaced workers (from 65% to 75%), speeds payment, and requires states to set up group coverage options, locking private insurance in as the channel for this public benefit while making it more affordable for workers.

The bill grants a legal safe harbor from shareholder lawsuits for decisions to keep jobs in the US — a litigation shield that benefits directors personally while advancing the policy goal of keeping jobs at home.

industries.industry: Workers' retraining providers and state workforce agencies
industries.note: Retraining funding would have doubled to $440 million and new administrative money ($300 million for 2004–2006) would have flowed to states for enrollment help and interim coverage.
